text.p: Reform of Singapore's compulsory Central Provident Fund (CPF) retirement programme will have a tremendous effect on the local fund management market, senior executives said on Monday.

"In terms of the restrictions of the past they have been lowered dramatically and the market has opened up tremendously," Patrick Tan, investment director of Rothschild Asset Management (Singapore) Ltd, told a news conference.

Tan was speaking at the launch of a new investment fund from life assurer John Hancock, the first in a series of sectoral funds planned by the company to exploit new CPF investment rules which became effective on January 1.

Rothschild is fund manager for the Pacific Finance Fund, which invests in bank and financial institution stocks, and the Pacific Harvest Fund, which invests in the top 88 equities in Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Korea and Taiwan.

Both form part of an umbrella fund, said Malcolm Arney, president and chief executive officer of John Hancock in Singapore. He said there would be a flurry of activity arising from the reform of the CPF.

Industry sources say they expect an additional Singapore $350 million to be committed to investment funds in 1997 after reforms reduced the entry level at which CPF funds can be invested in a broad range financial instruments.
Arney said Hancock was investigating funds for a range of economic sectors, but declined to give details. All would be approved CPF investment instruments, he said.
Singapore's regulatory authorities had approved one other fund and it would be launched separately, Arney added.
Once complete, the fund network would enable investors to switch between sectors to maximise returns, he said.
